p: Sure.
And so we have dozens of large class cases that attorneys are handling and in various stages of the process whether that’s in the data analytics process or in the settlement negotiations process.
Could you give me like a general number? Could you– how many cases are in court? How many cases are in negotiations? Like, could we– you know, I’m sure you have that number somewhere?
We’d have to follow up with you to give you a precise number. I could say today that it’s several dozen, but we can definitely get those breakdowns for your office.

I would appreciate that. And then I am concerned about the backlog, and you know, I know the Commissioner and you are deeply committed to this work. You wouldn’t be doing it otherwise. And to say that maybe in a year we might be in a better position is a little concerning to me because, you know, this is a priority for all of us, and I’m wondering if you had more resources staffing up sooner, like instead of hiring 12– 10

investigators, you hired 15. Obviously, that backlog would reduce quicker. Is that a fair statement?

One point I would make, and then I’ll turn it over to the Deputy Commissioner is, you know, we do have the– it’s a good problem to have, but we’re such a lean agency that the same folks who are doing those investigations are interviewing candidates, and they’re going to spending a lot of the summer both full steam ahead on their cases and full steam ahead on interviewing candidates and they’re going to keep interviewing through the rest of the year. So, the reality is that again, new lines, it’s a wonderful problem to have, but it does– there are only so many people we can operate, and we really designed the 181 very– OMB would not have authorized that headcount if we didn’t show them in granular detail that we have the capacity to bring those folks on. So, I’m not saying– you know, we could have conversations about what additional capacity would mean in hiring, but I just want to say that there is– there are operational limits on how many folks we can bring on. You know, if we could hire a million people tomorrow, we would not actually be able to close the backlog tomorrow.

That’s right. Just in terms of the resources to train people. This is the right number to be able to absorb new staff, to have them learn and follow our procedures for investigations and to ultimately continue delivering the high level of service that we offer workers.

Well, we’ve heard– you choose one industry, deactivation, right? So, you know, we’ve heard from the deliveristas that every day 200-300 people are banging down their door about deactivation. So, they don’t have capacity to do it. So how do we support them to ensure that they, you know– they could maybe a front line person to limit the number of cases that are coming to you. You do have resources in the budget to help organizations like that who are really on the front lines trying to help?
We have resources in the budget to make sure that we are– we have the staff to meet those needs.
Right.

We’re also working very closely with outside partners to make sure that

there’s an orderly process, people know their rights. Do you want to talk a little bit about deactivation implementation?

Sure. And just to first say, WJP and all of our community partners do extraordinary work. They are a critical part of the worker protection infrastructure, and you know, definitely want to see them continue to be supported to do that work so that they can continue to refer us cases so that we can continue to refer them cases on matters outside of our jurisdiction. It’s really critical. And we will, you know, continue to work with organizations who are working with delivery workers to make sure they’re able to get delivery workers to us so that we can pursue those deactivation matters for them.
So, you have no money in the budget to give– to subcontract them to do this work. Is that what I hear you saying?
We do not manage those contracts, that’s right. That runs through– Carlos should speak to this, but yeah.

Well, that’s correct. The money that we were allocated was for

personnel services and to increase the agency’s capacity.
Right.

I recognize your point and in full agreement that over the past 10 years the agency has had historic disinvestment, but that’s why we’re incredibly excited with what the mayor has done. Obviously, with the support of the Council and our allies that you’re bringing up in this conversation, too, Chair, to bring us to a place where we can meet our mandates and hopefully grow even further as new mandates come.

I mean, I do care. I care about the street vendors, and they– they may not come to DCWP right away. They may need an organization like the Street Vendor Project to ferret out what’s an appropriate case to come to. They have the relationships. It’d be great to see funding from the agency. It just says we know we’re going to have to enforce these laws, but we know these are really culturally competent organizations who are on the ground who are going to be able to figure out what should come to us and what shouldn't. Shouldn’t

there be resources from your agency to go directly to them?

Well, I would say, Chair, that that partnerships exists and will only grow, and we plan to work closely with Street Vendor Project and our new Executive Director for Street Vendor Services will to go directly to street vendors, to go to the places where they’re vending to ensure that they understand about what services and licenses are available by the agency. So, that’s our current PS allocation is, and again, we look forward to having these conversations if we’re going to need more resources eventually.
Yeah. I mean, [inaudible] but Carlos, you wouldn't disagree that they need resources too, right?

I– no, thank you. Thank you, Chair. Sorry, I was distracted. I wouldn't disagree that I’ve had conversations directly with WJP and other organizations. I know that they have conversations directly with the Council themselves over discretionary funding. So, I understand that those [inaudible] too. I just can

only speak to our budget and our resources and what we’ve been allocated.

And I would just add to that, Council Member– Chair, right, we do not give money for those organizations, but I will say though is that I really believe that it is symbiotic in a way. We are working closely, for example, with Street Vendor Project to get the word out this summer about getting off the wait list and getting a license. That is going to provide a real value proposition for the Street VEndor Project to all the vendors out on the street. Similar with Workers Justice Project, NYWJ [sic], they’re going to work with their members to explain to them deactivation protections. We’re going to work with NYCHA and WJP. I think the more that we partner closely with these organizations, the more that they’re going to be able to offer value to their members, and I hope that creates a virtuous cycle. These organizations gain more visibility and reach and that we can do the same.

Commissioner, I couldn't agree more with that statement, and I– you know, I just would say that– I know we have

colleagues that have questions. But I’d love to see if there’s a way we can get them direct funding to do that, because you know, I’ver heard directly from all of them whether it’s Worker Justice Project like you mentioned or the Street Vendor Project we just talked about who, you know, there are more members coming to them than they have their resources to handle, and While you’ll be the agency in power to rep– to protect their members as well as all the consumers out there, there’s a– there’s not as many resources that they can turn to to be able to do this work and we’d love to see the administration play a vital role in getting those resources to them.

I hear you on that, and to be clear, and I think I speak for everyone here, we could not do our job. We could not do the worker protection we’ve done without partners like WJP and NYCWA sic. I totally agree on the vital role these organizations play.
And thank you. I’lll turn it back over to Chair Lee.

Great. Just also want to recognize we’ve been joined by Council Member Ariola online and we– and Tiffany Cabán, hello. So,

we are going to start with Deputy Speaker followed by Council Member Banks.

Thank you. Hello. Just a macro question around the racial equity plans. So, how does DCWP define equitable enforcement, and what metrics does the agency use to determine whether enforcement practices are being applied fairly across communities?

Well, I would make two points because I think this is a critically important issue. The first is that we know that some of the worst economic abuses are targeted at New Yorkers of color, Black and– primarily Black and Brown New Yorkers and immigrant New Yorkers. That is why I am fully committed not only to continuing to vigorously enforce our laws, but making sure that our enforcement actually reflects where abuses are happening throughout our city. There have been studies not in New York, but nationwide that consumers of color, for example, are less likely to report violations to government agencies. What does that mean? It means the government agencies are less likely to hold accountable those who prey on communities of color. That is not acceptable. My

commitment at DCWP is to make sure we’re serving everyone in New York City, especially those being harmed the most by these abuses, and that is why we take so much pride in our outreach efforts. We are aiming to do the two events a day, more than 700 events every year. We go to every borough, every community. And that I say to every group, if you don’t feel comfortable filing a complaint with the government, you can go to Worker Justice Project. You can go to Make the Road, go to another group, file a complaint with us. It is critical that we not only kind of sit in our downtown office waiting for complaints, that we go out in the community and make sure that we’re serving people who are most targeted by economic predation.
So, back to the racial equity plans, though, like what goals has DCWP put forward that matches what you just said?

Well, a key goal– and this came up in the Core report that came out very recently is on youth financial empowerment. You know, the fact of the matter is, we’re the beginning of summer. We know that a lot of young New Yorkers are going to have their first jobs, and they’re

instantly going to be targets for predatory fin [sic] tax, predatory actors are going to try to separate them from their paychecks. One of the points that was made by Core was that DCWP should really step up its financial empowerment work, especially its youth financial empowerment work including in partnership with Kids Rise. I could not agree more with that. We’re never going to have the resources to take down every bad actor, even with the Council’s generous proposal this morning. So that’s why I think it’s really important to empower people in school banking, which was another Core recommendation. It’s something we are implementing. Youth financial empowerment, we’re going to reach every school district by the end of FY29. So, I thought the Core report was right on point in terms of our goals and how we’re going to meet them over the years to come.

And just to go back to equitable enforcement, because you answered that question by primarily talking about workers, but businesses– so, has DCWP conducted any geographical or demographical [sic] analysis of where violations, inspections, and enforcement actions are concentrated citywide? So, that’s what I’m talking about.
I see– I apologize.
Because for me, because I think about budget equity. We’re at a budget hearing. What I want to know and I’m always interested in is where is the city also generating revenue?
Yes.

Are you only generating revenue in certain communities over others? And so that is sort of the source of my first question, coupled with the other one about if you have any geographical or demographical [sic] analysis of where violations are occurring across New York City?

I don’t have it at my fingertips. I do believe we have pretty good analyses of where we’re seeing violations throughout the city, but I also want to be clear and you know, repeat what I said earlier. I don’t believe in gotcha enforcement, especially with the small businesses. We’ve seen an exodus of small businesses last year under the final year of the Adams administration. We’re really trying to reverse that. I was very proud that Mike's team, the General

Counsel team, returned more than half a million dollars to immigrant-owned small businesses. First enforcement action in our history to do that– who were ripped off by Hungry Panda, a delivery app. So, I’m happy to get you additional data on where enforcement is, and I–
[interposing] Yes, I would love to– similar– I asked DOT a similar question. Like, if you do have a map–
[interposing] Yeah.
of where you’re primarily finding certain businesses across New York City, that would be helpful. Thank you.
I am happy to see what we can get you on that. I think we do– I think we do have that. We will follow up.
Okay, great. Council Member Banks?

Thank you, Chairs and Commissioner to your team. When it comes to Local Law 168 which went into effect on May 27th, just recently, which requires tax preparers to provide consumers with itemized feed and disclosures before and after services are rendered. Want to know

what steps has DCWP taken to educate preparers and consumers about these new requirements to ensure compliance with the law.

Yeah, we take this incredibly seriously. It’s– you know, we see so much predation in the tax prep space. It’s one reason why we were so aggressive this year in promoting our free tax prep and doing a warning blitz, I think the first in our history to every licensed tax prep provider in the city that we are looking at for violations. Mike, do you want to share more on our implementation?
No. It’s a very important topic and something that we always have our ear to the ground on. You know, we had a case against Rocket Tax last year.
Right, yeah, okay.

That, you know– and we’re always looking for compliance in that– for that settlement. And we’re always looking for new targets. You know, one of the great things, we have a consumer services unit that is our ear to the ground for all consumer complaints, and we look at the trends, both in terms of who are potential

targets in this, using tax prep in all our categories. Like who are individuals businesses that see are repeat violators of the laws and rules we enforce, and what are the new scams that we didn’t even know about but people on the street are telling us. So, we always encourage people to go directly to our website and file complaints. That’s really the grift for how we determine how we’re going to direct our enforcement.
Thank you.
Council Member, I would also–
[interposing] Thank you for that response. Let me just get my questions out and then you can–
[interposing] Sorry.

You can chime in on the next one if you want. While tax season is technically over, many New Yorkers continue to file extensions, amendments on their returns and they utilize the tax preparation services throughout the year, has DCWP already begun consumer outreach regarding Local Law 168? And if so, what has the

outreach looked like and what lessons has the agency learned thus far?

Yeah. I’ll ask Carlos to describe a little bit of some of the specific outreach, but if I may just a brief point, public service announcement for everyone. Our New York City free tax prep serves over 100,000 New Yorkers every year. No fees. No fines. No nothing except tax help.
Right.
Is available year-round.
But there’s a large percentage of folks who don’t take advantage of that–
[interposing] Absolutely, Council Member.
[inaudible] yes.

And Council Member, I was going to mention that I know we’re updating our educational materials for businesses as well, and we should be distributing those soon so they can understand their obligation under the law.

Okay. And then on the educational materials, we’re hoping that they’re

obviously multilingual. Obviously, the– you talked about the public awareness campaigns, and what partnerships are you going to be forming to develop to ensure that both consumers and tax preparers understand their rights and the obligations of Local Law 168?

Well, traditionally, you know, our outreach model is based on deep ties with local community-based organizations being able to plug into their regular membership and convenings of community members. So, I think we’re going to activate those again. You know, typically throughout the tax season we hit hundreds of events to help educate consumers and that even starts before the tax season. So, I think we’re going to plug into similar aspects and working with also business associations and their representatives. I think it’s been a trusted model for us in our outreach.

Excellent. And what will compliance monitoring look like with Local Law 168? What enforcement tools are available to address violations, and has the agency identified any implementation challenges that may require additional

staffing, resources or legislative changes moving forward?

I think we have thanks in part to the law and to the investment by the mayor. I actually think we have strong authority and capacity to take these on. One technique we’ve done in the past which has been effective is sweeps where we do a broad prep [sic], because precisely for the reason you said. Most New Yorkers are still using private preparers.
Correct.
Many of them are breaking the law. You know, when we do a sweep we’re sending a message that we’re looking across the marketplace. You want to add to that?

Right and there are two ways we can conduct this. We have a Field Enforcement Division. People are out in the street every day as we’re speaking going to business, making sure they’re complying with the consumer face– mostly consumer-facing laws and rules of the city. And so we have people around tax seasons, we have sweeps of those and making sure that tax preparers are complying with the specific laws and rules that they

need to comply with. Then we have lawyers, you know, back in the office–
[interposing] Right.
who are looking at those complaints, like I mentioned before, Council Member, and saying which businesses should we be taking a deeper look into.
Okay. Well, thank you for your responses and looking forward to continue working with you. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you. We have Council Member Pierina Sanchez followed by Council Member Krishnan.

Thank you, Chair, and good morning. First, I just want to start with expressing how exciting it is to see the agency’s trajectory these last six months. I think any mayor, any executive envisions a commissioner like you when they win office, coming in with a track record of success, but also an ambitious vision for the agency and a readiness to roll up your sleeve with the team that is there. I just want to

congratulate you on everything that you guys are all doing together for New Yorkers. I’m going to do the thing where I ask all my questions up front and then hope that there’s time for a response.
Okay. We’ll take notes.

Thank you. So, to start, DCWP– I mean, I’m biased. You are my favorite. You're one of my favorite agencies. Don’t tell HPD. You’ve just been such a fantastic partner on reforming the street vending system in New York City. Special shout out to Carlos Ortiz and everyone back there. We have really reframed this problem together in New York City, and I appreciate it. So, my first question here is, you know, while I appreciate– I’m very– was very happy to see significant investments for the implementation of street vending reform. I remain concerned that the piece that DCWP has around processing 10,500 new general vendor licenses is still too low. I understand that there’s only six new staff that are going to be added for fiscal year 27. So, I just want to understand the plans for processing these new applications per Local Law 54 with this staffing.

Question two, the new licenses that are being made available in January will be the first change to the general vendor cap since 1979. So, the questions are when the new wait list opens, how will DCWP prioritize the new general vendor licenses? Do you have a sense of the criteria the agency will be using? And how can we ensure that licenses are getting to the hands of the street vendors who have been waiting for decades? And the third one on street vending is outreach. The Chair touched on this a bit regarding Street Vendor Project and our partners on the ground, but I suppose my question is whether there’s any dedicated staff within the agency across the 189 new lines that you mentioned in your opening specifically for outreach? And then, as you know, Commissioner, I am ecstatic about the Click to Cancel rule and that the momentum you– the agency has on this policy. You know, I speak for myself and I know many New Yorkers who are just so freaking annoyed by companies that make it impossible to leave subscriptions, that harass you even after you’re gone, but really trap New Yorkers into subscriptions that they don’t need. So, just a status update on what– where we are with the proposed rules and is

there any staffing associated with implementation of that new rule. Thank you.
Okay, thank you,Council Member.
Two seconds to spare.

That was great. I’m going to run through each one and we’ll see how I do, okay, and Carlos can back me up. Alright. Licensing staffing– we are confident we have the capacity in our licensing division to hit the ground running this summer on getting the general vendor licenses out the door. We have an extremely efficient licensing division, and I’ll just say, you know, average wait time of four minutes when you're in the office, four days for processing. Typically most– above 90 percent of licensees now apply online. We recognize many street vendors are going to prefer the in-person option, and that is why we asked for and received six new lines for FY27. We are confident we’re going to be able to meet those needs to continue– you know, outstanding, I think the best in the city for licensing service to our smallest small businesses and our newest licensees. With respect to the wait list and how to prioritize. We’re going to be

releasing rules on that in the next couple weeks. I could say as a general matter, Council Member, we’re going to start with about the 9,000 folks who are already on the wait list which was closed in 2016. Once we process those applications, we move on to creating a new wait list and we’ll start processing those applications. We’re going to put out the rule soon, but my commitment is to make sure this process is predictable, people understand it, people know that even if they don’t get a license in the first tranche, they know where they are in line. And that's really important to us. With respect to outreach, we really want to go big this summer. And Carlos will be able to add to this I think after I get through the questions. I know we’re meeting with you in a couple days about this. We’ve been working with Street Vendor Project, with the Office of Street Vending, the Small Business Services. We know that this is a community not used to being helped by the city. Usually when they interact with city officials, it’s police or other enforcement. We want to reach out to our street vendors with licenses and with information on how to obtain licenses. So, we are dedicating staff to outreach on that and Carlos can

share more. Last, but definitely not least, we’re incredibly excited about the Click to Cancel rule as I share your enthusiasm. It is a proposal right now. We are the first city in America to propose a rule like this. We’re very excited about it. We received a lot of comments. I don’t know the exact number, but I think one of the most interesting comments is from the Roosevelt Institute which estimated that this could save New Yorkers up to $160 million every year. That is the scale of tricks and traps we are facing. So, we’re extremely excited. The next step will be. We’re going to make a decision about whether to adopt the rule and make it final. Do you want to add a little bit to the outreach portion?

Yes, thank you, Commissioner. I think we’re already developing plans for how to meet street vendors where they are including by identifying high traffic areas where vendors are conducting their business activity. Our Community Affairs team is six members right now, but they burn a lot of shoe leather. I think they’re– I personally believe they’re the best outreach team in the city, and our overall External Affairs Division often contributes as well to helping out outreach

initiatives. So, I think we plan to be out there extensively over the course of the summer, also working with agency partners too to make sure that we have boots on the ground to accomplish our goals.
Thank you. There you go.
Thank you, Chair, chairs. Okay, next we have Council Member Krishnan followed by Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Chairs. Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner and all the whole team, thank you all so much for all your great work at DCWP and your leadership. Proud to see all that you're doing and to partner together. Deputy Commissioner, First Deputy Commissioner, Carlos Ortiz, also a constituent in Jackson Heights, too. So I appreciate you all. You’re paying close attention to the issues there from street vendors to taxi cab drivers, everything else. I just have a quick question. So, one is, you know, we’ve talked a bit about having the resources that you all need for the new legislation that we’ve passed. And so I just want to make sure. We’ve talked a lot about street vendor implementation. Very glad to hear that. I

know, Commissioner, we’ve spoken a bunch about taxi drivers, the deactivation bill that we passed and how important that is. So, I just want to make sure you all feel that you have what you need for the number of cases that will come in, the lookback period, and how that will be raised. You feel good with what you’ve got to unveil that program?

I do, Council Member. I really appreciate the question. I think it was probably apparent from the last hearing we had that my biggest concern actually going into the summer was how we’re going to make sure we can meet the Council’s mandate on the outstanding bill you championed on for-hire vehicle deactivation later in the year, at the end of the year, delivery worker deactivation. I do feel confident. Liz’s team is working very hard to put an infrastructure in place. You know, we’re going to see what the volume is. If it spikes much higher than we think, you know, we might have to revisit it, but at this point, based on our projections of staffing, we do have confidence we can meet those needs.

Great. And can you say a bit more about- is it going to be a new

staff, set of staff attorneys hired that would be focused on this in particular, or how– what would that staffing look like?
I’m going to turn that over to our person in charge of that.

Sure. Right now, we’re very focused on rule-making and being sure we can get a rule out that lays out some of the key details of how apps are required to handle the various– their various obligations under this law. We are looking to staff this law the way we have successfully enforced many of our laws with investigators trained to do the initial intake work, who often are able to successfully resolve a case without attorney involvement, and then moving to attorneys when that’s not possible. And we believe that we’re going to be able to be able to start successfully handling those cases.

Great. Very glad to hear it. And Commissioner, I’ll just say, too, any way that we can partner together, you know, to get the word out too in districts where there’s obviously high, you know, driver/resident populations, you know, partner with us, my office,

with NYTWA [sic]. Very happy to find any ways to get the word out there.
We would love to do that. We’re eager to get the word out. NYTWA’s [sic] been a great partner in this and we’d love to work with you further.

Absolutely. Well, thanks for your leadership and I know Carlos will follow up separately too on a couple of quality of life issues too in the district, and we want to [inaudible] with you all, too. So, appreciate your partnership there, too.
Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member.
Thanks.
Thank you. Council Member Wong followed by Council Member Cabán.

Thank you, Chairs. In my district there’s a big problem of unlicensed tow trucks, and the problem is this, whenever there’s an accident, the police is no longer required to show up at the scene. So we have these tow trucks that pop out of nowhere quite often with fake plates and

with a combination of coercion and threats, they were able to convince many of these drivers to let their cars be towed away without– they don’t know. The drivers don’t know that they’re fake, unlicensed or with fake licenses. So, this is only my fifth month at the job and I’m hearing like over a dozen of these complaints that their cars got towed away to some backyard shop and they’re being extorted on hundreds of thousands of dollars in storage fees and in repairs that they did not expect. So, can you talk about what is being done and how could your increase in headcount be able to step up your enforcement of checking their licenses? Thank you.

I’m very happy to, Council Member. I’m going to frame it up and then turn things over to our General Counsel including our– including our recent enforcement action against one of these unlicensed companies. Let me just start by saying this is a huge problem across the city, big problem in Queens. The– and one thing I really want to stress is, you know, we always– we want to educate consumers about this. We want to educate New Yorkers to use licensed tow providers, but one thing I always say to people is it is not on consumers to get this

right. You’ve just been in a car accident. Your car just broke down. You can’t realistically expect people to go to dcwp.gov and see if– .nyc.gov and see if they’re licnesed. So, my big focus is on making sure these unlicensed tow companies are held accountable. The onus has to be on the tow companies to stop operating illegally on our streets, not on consumers to do their own due diligence when they’re in some of the hardest moments of their lives.

Yeah, we take this very seriously. I mean, this is one of our core license categories that we get the most complaints about. Not just about unlicensed activity. In fact, often it’s from licensed actors who are overcharging. The Council has very wisely set very strict limits on how much tow companies can charge consumers, because it is such a precarious time for consumers as the Commissioner was alluding to and as you are referencing. So, we look through those complaints. We choose which ones are getting the most complaints and we focus our enforcement in that direction. We filed a case against Instant Recovery as the Commissioner alluded to in his opening testimony. We always have several major open tow investigations

ongoing. As far as unlicensed activity, that is a little trickier because it’s out on the street in real time. That’s something that we’re partnering with the New York Police Department to figure out what the best next steps are, and I will say it’s very important if you are getting complaints from constituents, we’re all ears, and there’s a lot of different avenues that you can approach. Individuals, you know, despite what the Commissioner said, can always go to DCWP, but you and your staff we’re always– Carlos, my team, we always want to hear what are the companies, because actually individual names with individual facts on the ground will always help sharpen our investigations.
Yeah, I’ll share the list with you based on the info I collected from my constituent complaints.
Great, thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member.
Thank you, Chair.

Thank you. Council Member Cabán followed by Council Member Aldebol.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thank you. Hello. You guys are my favorite agency. I don’t– I don’t need to couch it. My colleague over there, you can tell everybody. Also, thank you for–

[interposing] I will tell everybody now. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: I stand by it, whatever. Also, glad to see that you had Amazon cough up, what, close to $10 million in unpaid tickets. So I was happy to see that. Not going to be surprised that I want to ask about the Delivery Protection Act and sort of what that will cost moving forward. I know that– I heard testimony that you feel good about your ability to enforce the many laws that we have already passed and the ones that are coming into effect, but we want to do more. I think that, you know, we share the same ambition in being able to do more. We also know that there’s just so much that we get in return in terms of raising revenue and putting money back in people’s pockets. So, you know, at the hearing on Delivery Protection Act, you testified that you support the bill. Do you feel ready to– should it pass– enforce the licensing process and requirements that would come along with

that? Do you– with the numbers that you have, is that enough to enforce that bill, for example, or do you need more?

Well, thank you, Council Member. We enthusiastically support the bill. I mean, just yesterday we were discussing before this hearing the Supreme Court case around a company that tried to force for-hire vehicle– excuse me, last mile delivery workers into arbitration. This was in another state, but it just shows the scale of the worker exploitation we see all over the United States. Your bill would put a stop to that in New York City. With respect to the lines we need to enforce it, I believe we estimated we would need 19 lines. That was not included in the Executive Budget since it’s still– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Okay.
hasn’t passed. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Because we want to pass that soon.
Yeah, us too. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: So, it sounds like you could use some more money.

Yes.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay, that sounds good. I also want to ask, because again, we share the goal in being as ambitious as possible. You guys are very good at what you do. I know that there may be limits on what you can say about potential legislation or legislation that hasn’t even come before you yet. But what do you see as other potential areas of expanded regulation that you are currently concerned with?
